Four things the research keeps coming back to

No miracle products. These are the levers with real evidence behind them — the foundation everything else on this site builds on.

1

Keep them lean

The single strongest lifespan finding in dog science: in Purina’s 14-year study of 48 Labradors, dogs kept lean lived a median of 1.8 years longer and stayed healthier. You should be able to feel ribs under a thin fat layer.

2

Move every day

Muscle is a senior dog’s savings account. Daily walks, gentle hills and short play sessions protect joints, weight and brain. Little and often beats one long weekend hike — especially after age 10.

3

Test, don’t guess

From age 7–8, twice-yearly vet visits with bloodwork catch kidney, liver and thyroid trouble while it’s still cheap and treatable. Trends matter more than any single result — keep the reports.

4

Protect teeth, joints & brain

Dental disease seeds bacteria into the heart and kidneys. Joint pain quietly shrinks a dog’s world. And cognitive decline has early signs most owners miss. All three are manageable — if you start early.

The dog longevity drugs: LOY-001, LOY-002 & LOY-003

A San Francisco company called Loyal is developing the first drugs intended to extend lifespan itself — not treat a disease. Here is where each one actually stands with the FDA, in plain English.

LOY-002
FOR: SENIOR DOGS, 10+ YEARS, 14+ LB

A daily, beef-flavored pill that targets the metabolic changes of aging — designed to mimic some benefits of calorie restriction without feeding less. The lead program, and the one closest to market.

Closest to launch
  • Effectiveness (RXE)Accepted Feb 2025
  • Safety (TAS)Accepted Jan 2026
  • ManufacturingIn progress
  • Possible availability2026 (conditional)
LOY-001
FOR: LARGE & GIANT DOGS, 7+ YEARS, 40+ LB

An injectable that lowers IGF-1, the growth hormone linked to why big dogs age faster and die younger. If it works, it targets the breeds with the shortest lives — Great Danes, Bernese, Rottweilers.

FDA milestone reached
  • Effectiveness (RXE)Accepted 2023
  • FormVet-administered injection
  • StatusIn development
LOY-003
FOR: LARGE & GIANT DOGS, 7+ YEARS, 40+ LB

A daily pill version of the same IGF-1 approach as LOY-001 — same goal (slow the faster aging of big dogs), easier format for owners who prefer a tablet at home over injections at the clinic.

FDA milestone reached
  • Effectiveness (RXE)Accepted by FDA
  • FormDaily pill
  • StatusIn development

How we got here

2023FDA accepts LOY-001’s reasonable expectation of effectiveness — a first for a lifespan-extension claim.
Feb 2025LOY-002 clears the same effectiveness milestone for senior dogs of nearly all sizes.
Jul 2025STAY study finishes enrolling: 1,300+ dogs at 70 US vet practices — the largest trial in veterinary medicine.
Jan 2026FDA accepts LOY-002’s safety package, including data from 400+ dogs and doses up to 5× the intended strength.
2026 →Final manufacturing section to be submitted. Conditional approval could follow — full lifespan proof comes from STAY data over time.
Read this before you get excited: “Reasonable expectation of effectiveness” is not proof. No LOY drug is approved or on sale yet, and no completed trial has yet shown these drugs add years. Conditional approval, if it comes, means the FDA judges the drug safe and likely effective while long-term data is gathered. We track it because it’s historic — and we’ll say so plainly if the data disappoints.

Sources: Veterinary Practice News (Feb 2026) · Pulse 2.0 · Longevity.Technology · Loyal company announcements.

How long do dogs really live? Start with the breed.

Typical lifespan ranges for America’s most common breeds. Search, filter by size, and notice the pattern: the bigger the dog, the shorter the average life — which is exactly why large-breed owners have the most to gain from the new longevity science.

0 years5101518+ years

No breed matches that search yet. Try a different spelling — or check back as the database grows toward 100+ breeds.

Ranges are the typical published figures from breed references (AKC / PetMD) and veterinary sources, rounded to whole years. They describe populations, not your dog: weight, dental health, genetics and luck move an individual dog years in either direction. “Senior begins” is roughly the last quarter of the typical lifespan — when twice-yearly vet checks should start.

The Senior Dog Longevity Checklist

The whole evidence-based routine on one page. Print it, stick it on the fridge, and work through it with your vet. Free — no email required.

The daily basics Every day

  • Measured meals — no free-feeding for most seniors; you can’t manage what you don’t measure
  • Two or more short walks with sniffing time (sniffing is brain work)
  • A quick once-over: appetite, water intake, toilet habits — changes are early data
  • Five minutes of gentle play, training or a puzzle feeder for the brain
  • Fresh water checked and refilled; note if drinking suddenly increases

The weekly once-over Every week

  • Rib check: ribs easy to feel under a thin fat layer = healthy lean
  • Brush teeth or use a dental wipe (build toward daily)
  • Feel for new lumps; check ears, eyes and skin; photograph anything new
  • One small adventure: a new route, a dog friend, a car ride somewhere fun
  • Wash bedding and bowls — seniors fight infection less well

The vet partnership Twice a year, age 7+

  • Senior wellness visit with bloodwork (see our 7-tests guide)
  • Dental check — ask about cleaning before disease sets in
  • Honest review of weight, joints and pain: is your dog hiding stiffness?
  • Bring your notes and test reports; ask what changed since last time

The yearly reset Once a year

  • Re-check the food: does it still fit their age, weight and kidneys?
  • Review the budget: insurance, a savings pot, or both for senior costs
  • Refresh the home: ramps, non-slip mats, night lights on the route to the door
  • Update your “in case of emergency” card for whoever feeds your dog
  • Take a good photo together. Future you says thanks.

Product Lab

What we test, and how we judge it

The senior-pet market is full of hope in a bottle. The Lab’s rule is simple: if there’s no published evidence in dogs, we say so — however good the marketing is.

DNA & Biological Age Tests

Promising · useful if you’ll act on it

What they are

Cheek-swab kits (such as Embark’s Age Test) that estimate a dog’s biological age from DNA methylation — chemical marks on DNA that shift predictably with age, the same science behind human “epigenetic clocks.”

What we check

  • Published validation in dogs, not just human data
  • Whether the result would actually change care: screening start dates, weight targets, senior-visit timing
  • Breed and health-risk results included alongside age

Our rule

An age estimate is a planning tool, not a diagnosis. Worth the money if it changes what you do next.

Senior Dog Food

Evidence-based picks only

What actually changes after 10

Healthy seniors need more high-quality protein to fight muscle loss, not less — the old “low-protein senior diet” idea is outdated unless kidneys require it. Omega-3s (EPA/DHA), controlled calories and joint-supporting nutrients matter more than the word “senior” on the bag.

What we check

  • Named protein sources and digestibility data
  • AAFCO feeding-trial vs. formulated-only status
  • Calories per cup — the silent lifespan killer is the scoop

Our rule

We rank on nutrition evidence and feeding trials, never on which brand pays the best commission.

Joint & Brain Supplements

Mixed evidence · we sort it honestly

What the evidence says

Omega-3 fish oil has the strongest support for joints and inflammation. Glucosamine/chondroitin results in dogs are inconsistent. For the aging brain, medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) and antioxidant blends improved learning tasks in controlled senior-dog studies — early, but real, evidence.

What we check

  • Actual EPA/DHA dose per serving, not “proprietary blends”
  • Studies in dogs (not only rodents or humans)
  • Third-party quality testing (e.g., NASC seal in the US)

Our rule

Supplements support the basics — lean weight, movement, vet care. They never replace them.

About This Site

Why DogLongevityGuide.com exists

A new science needs a translator

Dog longevity has suddenly become real science: an FDA-track drug pipeline, a 1,300-dog clinical trial, DNA age clocks, and a generation of owners — the same people reading about human longevity — asking “what about my dog?”

The answers exist, but they’re buried in FDA filings, journal papers and vet-school language. This site exists to translate them for dog parents in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and other countries where dogs are family — and to be just as loud about what isn’t proven yet.

Where to go deeper

Primary sources we build on: Loyal’s FDA announcements and STAY study updates; Kealy et al., JAVMA (2002) — the Purina lifetime restriction study; the Morris Animal Foundation Golden Retriever Lifetime Study; and breed lifespan references from the AKC and PetMD. Every guide on this site links its own sources at the end.

Our editorial rules

  • Every science claim is sourced and date-stamped, so you can check it yourself.
  • No hype, ever. If a drug or product hasn’t been proven to extend life, we say exactly that.
  • Plain English first. If a term needs a glossary, we explain it in the sentence.
  • Corrections are public. If the FDA picture changes, the tracker changes — with the date shown.
  • Your vet outranks us. Always. We publish general information, not advice for a specific dog.
Important: DogLongevityGuide.com publishes general educational information about canine aging and longevity research. It is not veterinary advice and does not replace a relationship with your own veterinarian. Never start, stop or change medication, diet or treatment based on a website — including this one. Drug availability and FDA status change; check the tracker’s update date and your vet for the latest.
